title: AI Security Fundamentals
subtopics: Access control for models and tools
learning_outcomes: Explain aI Security Fundamentals and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in aI Security Fundamentals to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study aI Security Fundamentals within Responsible AI, Safety, Privacy, and Security. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Responsible AI is a lifecycle practice. Assess foreseeable harms, data handling, security boundaries, transparency needs, and routes for human accountability.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: AI security includes ordinary application controls and additional concerns such as untrusted model output, data leakage, prompt injection, model abuse, and tool permissions. Threat-model the whole pipeline rather than the model alone.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Authentication and authorization
items.text: Authentication and authorization is one of the concepts used to reason about ai security fundamentals. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Secure storage of credentials
items.text: Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant evidence and supplies it to a generator. Evaluate retrieval coverage, source relevance, grounding, and abstention separately; adding a retrieval step does not guarantee a supported answer.

items.title: Input validation
items.text: Input validation is one of the concepts used to reason about ai security fundamentals. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: API abuse prevention
items.text: API abuse prevention is one of the concepts used to reason about ai security fundamentals. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Access control for models and tools
items.text: Tool use lets a model request a defined operation, but the application should validate parameters and authorize the operation independently. Treat the model’s proposed action as untrusted input.

items.title: Dependency and supply-chain risks
items.text: Dependency and supply-chain risks is one of the concepts used to reason about ai security fundamentals. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Secure logging and monitoring
items.text: Operational monitoring combines service measures such as latency, errors, and cost with task-quality measures such as relevance or failure rate. Every alert should have a threshold, owner, and response plan.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what ai security fundamentals takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. Responsible AI is a lifecycle practice. Assess foreseeable harms, data handling, security boundaries, transparency needs, and routes for human accountability.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Copy the code into a local file named main.py and run `python main.py` with Python 3. Compare the printed output with the expected result documented here. This CodeLeaf content block is static; it does not execute the snippet in the browser and needs no external API key.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet or return to the small synthetic input, rerun it, and change one value at a time. Do not add real credentials, private user data, or untrusted code to the example.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: AI security includes ordinary application controls and additional concerns such as untrusted model output, data leakage, prompt injection, model abuse, and tool permissions. Threat-model the whole pipeline rather than the model alone. Next, connect this lesson to its prerequisite or next lesson and carry the same habit forward: define success, test a representative case, inspect failures, and document limitations.

content.task: Try it yourself: complete a small risk review for ai security fundamentals. Identify affected people, plausible failure modes, evidence needed, preventative controls, a residual risk, and the owner who would review the control after a change.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
troubleshooting: Use Python 3 and run the file from the folder where it was saved.
If output differs, restore the original input and compare one changed value at a time.
If Python reports a syntax error, check copied quotation marks, indentation, and whether the full code block was copied.
These examples require no external packages, network access, model credentials, or personal data.
